title: Where the test points sit decides what a test score can promise
summary: A split figure shows the parameter space of a simulated data set and colours each case train, validation or test. If every test case is surrounded by training cases, a good score certifies interpolation only. These figures also show what the corresponding trajectories look like in each split and a design that adds true extrapolation points.

media.alt: Scatter plot on dark background titled split geometry, random pool split. Horizontal axis initial temperature from 1000 to 1200 kelvin in five columns; vertical axis equivalence ratio phi from 0.5 to 1.5 in ten rows. Blue dots are training cases, five yellow dots validation, five red dots test, all inside a shaded rectangle that is the convex hull of the training points.

read_the_figure.question: Do the test cases lie inside the region the model was trained on, or outside it?
read_the_figure.axes: Horizontal: initial temperature T0 in kelvin (1000 to 1200 in steps of 50). Vertical: equivalence ratio phi (0.5 to 1.5). Each dot is one simulated case; colour is its split. The shaded rectangle is the convex hull of the training points.
look_at: Counts in the legend: 40 train, 5 validation, 5 test in the random split. 50 cases make a 5 by 10 grid, and the random draw leaves holes in the training grid.
The title states the consequence: every test point lies inside the train hull, so the score measures interpolation only.

In the structured design (marked as never run), nine test points are special: three green diamonds inside the hull at T0 = 1025 K, and six purple diamonds outside it at T0 = 1250 K with phi at 0.35 to 0.45 and 1.55 to 1.65. Those six test extrapolation by construction.

The trajectory bundles figure draws the same cases as curves: rows are temperature and three species, columns train, validation and test, with training curves in grey behind every column. Three groups of ignition times (about 0.05, 0.15 and 0.3 milliseconds) are visible in every column.
Check that test and validation curves fall inside the cloud of grey training curves: if they do, the test is an interpolation in curve space too.
read_the_figure.proves: A random split can only show interpolation within the sampled box. It cannot show how a model behaves at a new temperature or equivalence ratio. A structured split that places test points outside the hull is the only way a figure can support an extrapolation claim.
if_wrong: Test points inside the hull and the report says 'generalizes to new conditions': the claim is stronger than the figure.
A test set of five points: a single point is 20 percent of the score, so the result is dominated by chance.
Neighbours of a test point in the training set one grid step away: the test is nearly a leaked copy of training.
A design labelled 'never run': it is a plan; no result belongs on it.
must_check: That the split counts are printed.
That the hull (or the range) of the training set is drawn.
That extrapolation points, if claimed, are outside it by a stated margin.
That the same split is used for every model compared.

terms.meaning: Cases used to fit, to tune and to finally report; the test set is touched once.
The smallest convex region containing all training points; here a rectangle.
Test inside, respectively outside, the region spanned by training data.
The fuel-to-oxidizer ratio relative to the exact stoichiometric mixture; phi = 1 is stoichiometric.
The temperature at time zero of each simulated case.
Information from the test set reaching the training process, for example through near-duplicate cases.

remember: A score on test points inside the training hull certifies interpolation only.
Test sets with few points have large sampling error; say how many.
Extrapolation must be built into the split; a random split cannot test it.
Draw training curves behind validation and test curves to see whether they lie within the training cloud.
A design that has not been run has no results.

steps.title: Is a point inside the training hull?
steps.note: For a rectangular grid the hull is just the bounding box, so the test is two inequalities per axis: T0 within 1000 to 1200 K and phi within 0.5 to 1.5.

steps.title: Distance to the nearest training case
steps.note: Scaling each axis by its range makes distances comparable. This number, not just inside or outside, is what should accompany an extrapolation claim.

steps.title: Noise of a score from five test points
steps.note: With five test cases a pass-fail score is uncertain by more than 0.2. For a continuous error the standard error is the standard deviation divided by the square root of five.

steps.title: Ignition-time groups as a check on coverage
steps.note: The three clusters of sharp rises seen in every column of the bundle figure are three regions of this function. Test curves that fall in the same clusters are interpolation in curve space; a curve in a new cluster would be a real extrapolation.

worked.title: Normalized distance of the extrapolation points
worked.problem: The training ranges are T0: 1000 to 1200 K and phi: 0.5 to 1.5. A test case at (1250 K, 1.65) has nearest training case (1200 K, 1.5). Compute its normalized distance and compare with an interpolation test at (1200 K, 0.72) whose nearest neighbour is (1200 K, 0.61), one row away.
worked.answer: 0.29 against 0.11: the extrapolation point is about 2.6 times farther from its nearest training case, yet still only a modest step outside the hull. A hull test and a distance test answer different questions, and the distance should be reported.

analyze.q: The random split has five test points inside the hull. Which statement can the test score support: 'works at new T0 and phi' or 'works between sampled cases'? Why?
Why are training curves drawn in grey behind the validation and test columns?
The extrapolation points are at 1250 K, only 50 K beyond the hull. Is that a strong test? How would you make it stronger?

evaluate.q: A reader sees only the random-split figure and is told the model is validated. List three questions you would ask.
Is it acceptable to show a split design that was never run next to real results?

create: Design a leave-one-temperature-out split and draw it in the same style, with hull and counts.
Create a figure panel that adds the nearest-training distance of each test point as a number printed next to its dot.

checks.q: What does the shaded rectangle show?
checks.answer: The convex hull of the training points: the region over which the model is interpolating.

checks.q: Test at T0 = 1225 K, phi = 1.0. Inside the hull?
checks.answer: No: 1225 K is above 1200 K, so it is an extrapolation.

checks.q: Why can five test points not support a precise accuracy claim?
checks.answer: Only six possible fractions (0, 0.2, ... 1.0) exist, and each point moves the score by 0.2.

checks.q: A random split gives a better score than a structured one. Which is the honest measure of generalization to new conditions?
checks.answer: The structured one, because its test points include real extrapolation; the random one measures interpolation.

checks.q: Propose a split that tests whether the model works at a new equivalence ratio but known temperatures.
checks.answer: Remove all training cases with phi in a band (for example 0.9 to 1.1) at every T0 and test only there; the hull then has a gap in it, and the distance to training is measurable.
